extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics (writers and critics of epic and tragic poetry)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive rules and quality criteria for composing and evaluating epic and tragic poetry (diction, unity, measure, incidents, and representation), as given in a classical treatise on poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of uncommon expressions in moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words, metaphors, extended words, and everything beyond a proper word are 'uncommon' and must be intermixed in moderation; a poem composed entirely of them would be a riddle or a barbarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix uncommon expressions with common expressions to avoid obscurity or barbarism; preserve a medium in all parts so that diction neither becomes ridiculous nor merely ordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between uncommon forms and perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words, metaphor, ornament, and other uncommon forms render a poem neither vulgar nor poor, while common expression gives perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extensions, contractions, and alterations to increase perspicuity and freedom from vulgarity; do not overuse brilliant diction in places where it obscures sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improper use of expressive forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The person who uses foreign expressions, metaphors, etc. improperly will produce the same effect as one who uses them to excite laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper command and measured use are required; employing these devices without skill or purpose is a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor as sign of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest of all (devices) is the command of metaphor; to be happy in the metaphors we employ is the same as to have a correct discernment of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor indicates a correct understanding of the abstract nature of things and should be cultivated as a mark of poetic facility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction/forms to genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Double words are best adapted for dithyrambics, foreign for heroic, and metaphor for iambic poems; iambic, which imitates conversation, suits common, metaphor, and ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the kinds of words and figures suited to the particular species of poem; in heroic works a wider range may be employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (narrative should be dramatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative and imitation in verse ought to put together dramatic stories as in tragedy, relating to one whole and perfect action having a beginning, a middle, and an end; compositions ought not to resemble histories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select one principal action for coherence; avoid composing a poem as a mere chronological catalogue of events without a unifying end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a manageable part of a larger subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than attempting to celebrate an entire large subject (e.g., the whole war), the poet should select one part for his subject to avoid confusion or excessive length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing a portion allows unity and focus; Homer is praised for selecting a part of the war rather than the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic should have the same essential forms as tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic poem ought to have the same forms as a tragedy: simple, complex, moral, or pathetic; its parts (except melody and scenery) ought to be the same, possessing peripeteia, recognition, and passion, and be noble in sentiment and diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic poets should aim for peripeteia, recognition, passion, and nobility of sentiment and diction — qualities exemplified by Homer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and measure suited to genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic differs from tragedy in length and in measure; the beginning and the end ought to be seen at one view, and the composition's length should allow that (roughly equal to the number of tragedies recited at one hearing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the poem's length lets a reader/listener apprehend its whole at a view; avoid extreme brevity (mutilation) or excessive length (confusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes and variety in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry can introduce numerous and different episodes, representing many parts as proceeding at once to increase magnificence, provided the episodes are agreeable to the central action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes may diversify the poem but must have sufficient similarity or relation to avoid satiating the audience or breaking unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate poetic measure: heroic for epic
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic verse is best adapted for epic poetry; to imitate by narrative in other measures would appear unsuitable. One should not mix measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign the measure that fits the poem's nature; heroic is 'nervous and lofty' and accommodates foreign words and metaphors well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize poetial authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should himself say as little as possible; he should introduce characters who have manner and make them speak for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show rather than tell; let characters' speech and manner carry the imitation to avoid heavy authorial exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of the marvelous must suit medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ought to produce the wonderful, but that which is contrary to reason is more suitable to an epic poem because in epic we do not see the actor; the wonderful is at all times pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may include events beyond theatrical plausibility; embellishment (adding) in storytelling is permissible to please, but keep it credible in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer credible impossibilities to incredible possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: With reference to poetry, the credible impossible is preferable to the possible and incredible; choose incidents impossible in fact but that resemble truth rather than possible events unlikely to be believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for incidents that, though extraordinary, feel likely within the poem's world; this better secures the reader's belief and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unreasonable parts within the drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories ought not to be composed of unreasonable parts; the chief care should be to represent nothing as without a reason; if something unreasonable exists it must be outside the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't place inexplicable or absurd elements on stage; if necessary for the plot they should be made plausible by the story or kept off-stage (as in examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish diction in inactive parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour his diction in the inactive parts, such as exhibit neither manner nor sentiment, because very brilliant expressions rather obscure manner and sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate phrasing for parts where it enhances rather than obscures character or feeling; use clarity where action or manner must be visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of imitation of things
rubrics_metrics.description: Since a poet is an imitator he will represent things either such as they are or were, such as people call them or they appear, or such as they ought to be; these are related in common expressions, in foreign terms, or in metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you imitate reality, common opinion, appearance, or ideal, and choose diction and figures of speech appropriate to that mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish errors arising from art vs accident
rubrics_metrics.description: The error attendant upon poetry is twofold: one which arises from itself (inventing what is beyond its power) and the other which proceeds from accident (improper choice or ignorance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing or defending a poem, determine whether faults are due to violating artistic rules or to accidental ignorance or poor choice, as the blame and remedies differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify departures from fact by poetic end or convention
rubrics_metrics.description: If the poet represents men 'as they should be' (Sophocles) or 'as they were' (Euripides), or follows common opinion (myth), he may defend departures from literal fact; nature at large supplies materials and the poet may combine perfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genre conventions or moralizing aims to justify idealized representation; criticisms that a poem depicts impossibly excellent persons can be answered by poetic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine and interpret ambiguous expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some objections are refuted by reference to accent, pointing, ambiguity, or habit of expression; when a word appears contradictory, examine in what sense it is significant in the expression before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully analyze language, accents, idioms, and possible metaphorical senses before condemning a passage as wrong or absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge speech and action by situation and actor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a thing be said or done becomingly or unbecomingly ought to be considered by regarding not only the thing, but also the person who does or says it, to whom, at what time, in what manner, and for what end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual factors (speaker, addressee, timing, motive) can justify otherwise odd or improper utterances or actions in a poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refute criticisms by showing purpose or overall effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Many criticisms (impossibility, unreasonableness, badness, contradiction, or breach of artistic correctness) may be answered by showing reference to the art, to what is better, or to common opinion; twelve types of answers correspond to the criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending a passage, explain its role in producing the poem's intended effect (e.g., to astonish, to reveal character) and whether it adheres to artistic principles or serves a greater good in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate faults of poetry from faults of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive motion or gestures is a fault not necessarily of the poetry but of the representation; too much motion may result from poor performance rather than bad writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish textual/artistic defects from stage/performative faults when evaluating a play; avoid conflating actor excesses with poetic failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each art produces its proper pleasure (aim conformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and its species ought to produce only the kind of pleasure assigned to each (e.g., tragedy purifies passions, epic corrects manners); the work's success is measured by how well it attains its art's end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem by whether it achieves the particular cathartic, moral, or pleasurable end appropriate to its genre rather than by generic standards alone.
